title: E-Commerce API Design
description: Design a RESTful e-commerce API covering products, carts, orders, and checkout with proper HTTP semantics and resource relationships.

data.text: You are designing a public e-commerce API for a multi-vendor marketplace. The API must support product browsing, cart management, checkout, and order history. Third-party developers will integrate with your API, so consistency and discoverability matter.
REST APIs expose nouns as resources. Start by identifying the domain objects and their relationships. In e-commerce, the primary resources are Products, Carts, Orders, and Customers.

data.title: Primary resources
items: Products — catalog items with variants, pricing, and inventory
Carts — shopping carts scoped to a customer or session
CartItems — line items within a cart
Orders — immutable purchase records created from a cart
Customers — user profiles with shipping and billing addresses

data.text: Use hierarchical paths that reflect ownership. Sub-resources appear after the parent resource. Avoid verbs in URLs; use HTTP methods to express actions.

rows: New empty cart for session or customer

data.title: GET /products?category=electronics&limit=10&offset=0
data.content: Paginated product list with HATEOAS links for related resources.

data.text: Checkout is a state transition: Cart -> Order. The POST to /orders creates the order and invalidates the cart. This prevents double-checkout and keeps the order immutable.

data.title: Cart consumption
data.text: Never allow a cart to be reused after checkout. Return HTTP 409 Conflict if the cart is already converted to an order. This prevents accidental duplicate purchases.

data.title: POST /orders — Create order from cart
data.content: The request body references the cart ID and shipping address. The server validates inventory, creates the order, and decrements stock atomically.

items: Use an idempotency key (Idempotency-Key header or request body field) for all write operations
Return the cached response on duplicate requests instead of processing again
Store idempotency keys with a TTL (24-72 hours) to bound storage
Return 422 Unprocessable Entity if the idempotency key conflicts with a different request body

items.question: Should the API expose internal product IDs or slugs?
items.answer: Use opaque IDs (prod_881) in URLs. Slugs are nice for SEO but should be optional. If you support slugs, always fall back to the ID lookup if the slug changes.

items.question: How should I handle product variants?
items.answer: Treat variants as a sub-resource: GET /products/{id}/variants. Each variant has its own SKU and inventory. The parent product aggregates pricing and availability.

items.question: What status code should checkout return on success?
items.answer: 201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new order resource. The response body should contain the full order representation.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Model nouns as resources; use HTTP methods for actions.
Consume carts on checkout to prevent duplicate purchases.
Idempotency keys make payment integrations safe and retryable.
Use HATEOAS links to make the API self-documenting.
data.takeaway: A well-designed e-commerce API treats every resource as a noun, keeps URLs stable, and makes checkout a single irreversible state transition.
